nameStory: The 'reticulated' in this beetle's name comes from the Latin word for 'net-like,' referring to the delicate network pattern of veins visible on its wing covers. The 'net-winged' part of the name describes the family characteristic where these wing veins create a fine mesh pattern that looks remarkably like a tiny fishing net stretched across each wing. It's like nature gave this little beetle wings made of the most intricate lacework!
description: The Reticulated Net-winged Beetle is a small, soft-bodied beetle with distinctive orange and black coloring that warns predators of its bad taste. Its most striking feature is the intricate network of raised veins on its wing covers that create a net-like pattern, giving the entire beetle family its name. These day-active beetles are commonly seen on flowers and vegetation during summer months. Adults are typically about half an inch long with a somewhat flattened appearance and surprisingly soft wing covers unlike the hard shells of most beetles.

idTips.label: Net-like wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive raised veins creating a fine mesh or net pattern across orange wing covers - run your finger gently over them and you can actually feel the raised ridges

idTips.label: Orange and black banding
idTips.description: Body shows bright orange-red coloration with contrasting black bands or markings, creating bold warning colors that make it stand out against green foliage

idTips.label: Soft wing covers
idTips.description: Unlike most beetles with hard wing covers, these feel surprisingly soft and flexible to the touch - almost leathery rather than shell-like

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: The entire beetle appears somewhat pressed flat, with a noticeably less rounded profile than most beetles when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Daytime activity
idTips.description: Active during daylight hours on flowers and leaves rather than hiding under logs or coming out at night like many beetle species

habitat: Look for these beetles in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly areas with plenty of dead and decaying trees where they complete their life cycle. They're often found on flowers and foliage in forest edges, clearings, and woodland trails during summer. The presence of rotting logs and leaf litter is essential, as their larvae hunt small prey in the decomposing organic matter.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin emerging in late spring but are not commonly seen yet. Look for overwintering larvae becoming active in warming leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for adult beetles - look for them actively feeding on flowers and resting on vegetation during warm, sunny days. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Adults lay eggs in dead trees before dying off. Larvae begin their hunting phase in leaf litter as temperatures start to cool.
seasonality.winter: Larvae continue developing in protected spots within decaying logs and deep leaf litter. No adults visible during this dormant season.

funFact: These beetles are essentially tiny chemical warfare specialists - their bright orange and black colors warn birds and other predators that they taste absolutely terrible and may even be toxic, a survival strategy so effective that many harmless insects have evolved to mimic their warning colors!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the End Band Net-winged Beetle, which has similar coloring but different banding patterns. Memory trick: the Reticulated has more complex, 'reticulated' (net-like) patterns throughout, while the End Band has simpler bands mainly at the wing tips. Both share the telltale soft wing covers with raised vein networks that distinguish them from all other beetle families.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'banded net-winged beetle' is sometimes used for this species, but it can cause confusion since it's also applied to the closely related Calopteron discrepans. When identifying net-winged beetles, focus on the specific banding patterns rather than relying solely on common names, as several species share similar descriptive names.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the End Band Net-winged Beetle, the Reticulated species shows more complex banding patterns across the entire wing surface rather than having the distinctive dark bands concentrated mainly at the wing tips. Both species share the characteristic soft, net-veined wing covers and warning coloration, but the Reticulated typically has a more intricate overall pattern. The net-like vein structure is present in both, but the color pattern distribution is the key difference.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The End Band Net-winged Beetle is distinguished from its close relative, the Reticulated Net-winged Beetle, primarily by that telltale dark band across the wing tips.
